title: SoftBank market value halves from peak as AI fears grow
content:
SoftBank Group’s market value halved from its peak in June, as higher borrowing costs fuel investor concerns over the sustainability of its massive investments in artificial intelligence.
Shares of the Tokyo-based company fell 6.9% on Thursday, taking their drop from an all-time high struck on June 2 to 50%, with earnings from U.S. megacaps failing to ease the angst. After briefly overtaking Toyota as Japan’s biggest company four months ago, its market capitalization is now about ¥24.7 trillion ($157 billion), smaller than that of Hitachi and Recruit.
Global concerns over AI spending had accelerated after U.S.-based cloud-computing provider CoreWeave’s bonds fell to levels associated with distress, exposing financing risks across the industry.
“SoftBank’s vulnerability stands out as investors increasingly scrutinize the financial health of AI-related companies, given the group’s highly leveraged financial structure and growing borrowing costs,” said Kazuyuki Muramatsu, head of investment management at Nagomi Capital. If global sentiment toward the AI growth story turns sour, it may lead to valuation losses for SoftBank’s Vision Fund, which would in turn result in higher premium for future funding, he said.
The price to insure SoftBank’s debt against default has climbed, with credit-default swaps rising to the highest level in nearly four years on Tuesday.
With the company relying on debt financing for much of its investments across the AI ecosystem, ranging from infrastructure and energy to robotics, CoreWeave’s troubles dented confidence even in equity investors who had earlier focused on returns from SoftBank’s AI bets. The stock is Nikkei’s worst performer so far this month, down more than 30% and wiping out all gains from September.
Rising competition among AI models also remains an overhang. OpenAI, in which SoftBank has invested almost $65 billion, now faces more affordable Chinese rivals offering comparable performance.
SoftBank raised $11.1 billion in September via the largest corporate junk bond sale on record to finance founder Masayoshi Son’s big AI ambitions.

report.summary: SoftBank's market value has halved from its June peak as rising borrowing costs and CoreWeave's debt distress shake confidence in its heavily leveraged AI bets.
report.background: Under founder Masayoshi Son, SoftBank has repositioned itself as the world's most aggressive AI investor: roughly $65 billion into OpenAI, plus stakes across data centers, energy, robotics and chip designer Arm. That expansion was funded largely with debt — in September the group raised $11.1 billion in what was the largest corporate junk-bond sale on record. For most of 2025 that leverage looked like genius: in early June SoftBank briefly overtook Toyota as Japan's most valuable company. But the AI trade rests on cheap, abundant capital. As global borrowing costs stay elevated and investors start asking whether AI infrastructure spending can ever earn a return, the same leverage that amplified the rally is now amplifying the reversal — a pattern that echoes the 2000 dot-com unwind that nearly broke the company once before.
key_points: SoftBank shares fell 6.9% on Thursday, taking the drop from June 2's all-time high to 50%. At roughly ¥24.7 trillion ($157 billion), the company is now worth less than Hitachi and Recruit — a stark comedown for a group that briefly unseated Toyota as Japan's largest company just four months ago.

Credit markets are flashing warning signs. The cost of insuring SoftBank's debt against default hit a near four-year high this week. Because the group funds much of its AI expansion with borrowed money, every uptick in yields makes refinancing and future deals more expensive, squeezing the returns its bets must clear.

CoreWeave's troubles spread the fear. The U.S. GPU cloud provider's bonds fell to levels typically associated with distressed companies, exposing how much of the AI boom is financed with debt. For equity investors who had focused only on SoftBank's AI upside, that was a reminder of the downside.

There is a feedback loop risk. If sentiment sours, Vision Fund's private AI holdings get marked down, producing losses that raise the premium SoftBank pays on future funding — which in turn limits its ability to support the very companies dragging valuations down.

Competition is eroding the core thesis. OpenAI, recipient of nearly $65 billion of SoftBank money, now faces cheaper Chinese models with comparable performance. If AI capability commoditizes, the giant checks written for frontier labs look far harder to justify.
report.impact: SoftBank has become the market's de facto proxy for the AI trade, so its halving is a signal, not just a stock story. For the AI industry, the message is that capital is no longer free: financing-heavy infrastructure players — neoclouds, data-center developers, chip ventures — will face higher spreads and more scrutiny, likely accelerating consolidation toward cash-rich hyperscalers. For developers, tighter funding means fewer subsidized compute deals and slower price declines, though also more provider choice as weaker players are absorbed. For regular users, cheaper rival models keep consumer AI pricing low, but a prolonged capex pullback could slow product rollouts and reliability improvements. The key question is whether this is a valuation reset or the start of an AI credit cycle.
